script.opening: (Distressed, holding a cold flannel to her right eye, sounds nauseous.) "Doctor, my right eye is killing me — it came on a few hours ago, it's gone really red, my vision's blurry and there are these rainbow haloes round the lights. I've got a thumping headache and now I feel sick, I've actually been sick once. I wondered if it's a migraine or a bug, but the eye pain is unbearable."

facts.text: Started about 4 hours ago, in the evening after watching TV with the lights low. Came on over half an hour.
"Just the right. It's all misty with that eye." Rainbow haloes round lights. Left eye normal.

If asked to bring the eye close to the camera: "Like this?" — right eye very red around the coloured part; the right pupil looks bigger than the left. Too painful to keep it open long. Light makes it worse.
"A deep ache. No discharge." Pain 9/10 around and behind the right eye and across the forehead. Vomited once.

"I'm long-sighted, yes. Nothing new that I can think of, I'd have to look at my tablets." If she checks: started amitriptyline 10 mg at night 2 weeks ago for sleep and back pain. Also amlodipine. No allergies. No previous eye attacks.
"No" — no injury, no contact lenses, no recent eye surgery, no weakness or numbness, no neck stiffness or rash, never had migraines.
Lives with her husband, who doesn't drive at night. Daughter lives 10 minutes away. Eye unit is at the hospital 8 miles away.

In pain, frightened, wants relief: "I was hoping for something to stop it." If asked what worries her: "The pain, and my sight. I've never had haloes before." When told it's serious: "Is it serious?" then "Okay. What do I do?" If offered anti-sickness tablets or migraine treatment, she accepts gratefully (the trap).

ice.concerns: Unbearable pain; frightened by the haloes and the misty vision.

cues: "Rainbow haloes round the lights." — a key discriminator.
"I've been sick." — can mislead towards a bug.
"I'd have to look at my tablets." — a new medicine may be the trigger.

checkpoints.text: Recognises ACUTE ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA from the cluster (severe painful red eye, haloes, blurred vision, headache, nausea/vomiting, mid-dilated fixed/oval pupil, hazy cornea, hard eye — the signs confirmed in person, not on video) as a sight-threatening EMERGENCY

Avoids the pitfall of labelling the headache/vomiting as migraine or a GI bug — using the painful red eye with haloes as the discriminator and looking at the eye on video without delaying transfer for examination
Differentiates from other red eyes (conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis, scleritis, keratitis) by the distinguishing features

Identifies RISK factors/precipitants (hypermetropia, older age, female, East or South Asian family origin, dim light/pupil dilation, anticholinergic/sympathomimetic drugs, topiramate) including a relevant drug history
Arranges EMERGENCY same-day ophthalmology assessment immediately (sight-threatening within hours; needs urgent IOP-lowering and definitive treatment), with analgesia/antiemetic while transferring
Communicates calmly with a frightened patient in severe pain — explaining this is a serious eye emergency needing immediate specialist care and why it cannot wait
Balances urgency with reassurance (prompt treatment protects sight) and checks understanding of the plan

Safety-nets and arranges disposition: immediate transfer to eye casualty/ophthalmology, symptom relief meanwhile, advice not to drive, and clear escalation — emergency recognition and referral, not a migraine/antiemetic label

worked.txt: "I can see you’re in real pain, and I’m glad you came. This isn’t a migraine or a bug — the red painful eye, the haloes round lights and the sickness together point to a serious rise in pressure inside the eye, called acute glaucoma. It’s an emergency."

"On the screen your eye looks red, and the pupil may look bigger than the other one — I can’t check the pressure or how the pupil reacts over video, but with what you’re describing, that fits. Are you long-sighted, and are you on any tablets like older antidepressants, strong antihistamines or topiramate? … That can set it off."
"The pressure in the eye is high, and if it isn’t brought down quickly it can damage the sight — within hours, not days. So this needs the eye specialists today, right now, not a wait-and-see."
"I’m arranging for you to be seen at the emergency eye unit immediately — I’ll call ahead so they’re expecting you. Let’s also get something for the pain and the sickness while we sort transport."
"Don’t drive yourself — we’ll arrange how you get there. Take your glasses and your medicines list."
"The good news is that treated quickly, the pressure can be brought down and the sight protected. If you become much worse on the way, go straight to A&E. But the plan is: eye unit, now."

f.learning: ACUTE ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA is a sight-threatening ophthalmic EMERGENCY recognised by a cluster: a severely PAINFUL RED eye with BLURRED vision and HALOES around lights, plus HEADACHE and NAUSEA/VOMITING, and on face-to-face examination (a video call cannot confirm them) a fixed MID-DILATED (often oval) pupil, a HAZY/cloudy cornea and a hard eye, from a sudden rise in intraocular pressure. The key pitfall is being misled by the headache and vomiting toward a MIGRAINE, viral illness or GI bug while the eye complaint is downplayed — the discriminator is the painful red eye with haloes and blurring, so always ask about and examine the eye in anyone with headache/vomiting and unilateral eye pain. Distinguish it from other red eyes: conjunctivitis (gritty, discharge, normal vision), anterior uveitis (pain, photophobia, small/irregular pupil), scleritis (severe boring pain, autoimmune association) and keratitis (contact-lens-related, fluorescein uptake). Risk factors include HYPERMETROPIA (long-sightedness), older age, female sex, East or South Asian family origin (College of Optometrists), family history and a shallow anterior chamber, with precipitants of dim light/pupil dilation and pupil-dilating DRUGS (anticholinergics, tricyclics, some antihistamines, sympathomimetics, mydriatics, and topiramate, which can cause secondary angle closure within the first month) — so take a drug history. The action is EMERGENCY same-day ophthalmology assessment immediately, because sight is threatened within hours and urgent IOP-lowering and definitive laser peripheral iridotomy are needed (College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines; RCOphth 2022); in primary care, recognise rapidly, refer/transfer to eye casualty, and give analgesia/antiemetic while arranging it. Communicate calmly with a frightened, severely-painful patient, explain why it cannot wait, advise against self-driving, and reassure that prompt treatment protects sight.

knowledge.guideline: [1] RCOphth Management of angle-closure glaucoma (2022) · [2] College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines: primary angle closure · [3] Khurana AK et al., J Curr Glaucoma Pract 2012;6(1):6–8 (drug-induced angle closure) · [4] Topiramate SPC, section 4.4
knowledge.summary: A painful red eye with blurred vision, haloes, headache and vomiting is acute angle-closure glaucoma until proved otherwise. It is a same-day emergency: the pressure must be lowered within hours. Do not label it migraine or gastroenteritis, and send her to eye casualty now.

points.t: Severe unilateral eye pain, a red eye, blurred vision, haloes around lights, frontal headache, nausea and vomiting. On examination the cornea is hazy, the pupil is fixed and mid-dilated, and the eye feels hard. A video call can show redness and perhaps an abnormal pupil, but cannot confirm pressure or pupil reactions.

The College of Optometrists [2] classes acute angle closure as a same-day emergency. Raised pressure damages the optic nerve and can cause permanent visual loss within hours. The eye team lowers the pressure medically and then gives definitive treatment, usually laser peripheral iridotomy or lens extraction depending on the mechanism (RCOphth 2022 [1]), often treating the other eye too.

Headache and vomiting pull the diagnosis towards migraine, a viral illness or gastroenteritis. The discriminator is a painful red eye with reduced vision and haloes. Migraine does not make the eye red; conjunctivitis does not reduce vision or cause vomiting.

Anterior uveitis: pain, photophobia, small or irregular pupil. Scleritis: deep boring pain, often with autoimmune disease. Keratitis: pain, photophobia, contact lens wear. Conjunctivitis: gritty, discharge, normal vision, no severe pain.

Hypermetropia (a short, crowded eye), increasing age, female sex and East or South Asian family origin [2]. Precipitants: dim light and pupil dilation, including drugs with antimuscarinic or sympathomimetic effects, some antidepressants and antihistamines [3], and mydriatic drops. Topiramate can cause acute myopia with secondary angle closure, usually within the first month [4].
Recognise, explain and transfer immediately to the emergency eye service with a phone handover. Do not arrange routine follow-up or an optician appointment. She should not drive.

Acute angle closure versus migraine, gastroenteritis, uveitis, keratitis, scleritis and conjunctivitis.
Recognised a sight-threatening emergency and checked for drug precipitants.
Named acute angle-closure glaucoma and explained why headache and vomiting occur.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

model.text: Hello Mrs Voss, it’s Dr Hassan. I can see you’re uncomfortable. Tell me what’s happening.

My right eye is killing me. It came on a few hours ago, it’s gone really red, my vision’s blurry and there are rainbow haloes round the lights. I’ve got a thumping headache and I’ve been sick once. I wondered if it’s a migraine or a bug, but the eye pain is unbearable.
I’m sorry you’re in so much pain. I’m going to ask a few focused questions quickly, because the eye is the important part of this. Is that okay?
model.why: Keeps the consultation short and focused on the emergency

model.text: Yes, please.
Is it just the right eye? And if you cover the left eye, how well can you see with the right?
Just the right. It’s all misty with that eye.
Could you bring the camera close to your face, in good light, and look straight at it?
Like this?
That’s perfect. The right eye is very red and looks different from the left. I can’t measure the pressure or test your pupil properly on video, but what I can see fits with what you describe.
model.why: Describes findings honestly without over-claiming an examination

model.text: Is it gritty with sticky discharge, or more a deep, severe ache? Is bright light painful?
model.why: Discriminates from conjunctivitis, uveitis and keratitis

model.text: A deep ache. No discharge.

Did it start somewhere dim, like the evening or the cinema? Do you wear glasses for long sight? And have you started any new tablets or eye drops, including anything for mood, allergies, bladder or travel sickness?
model.why: Checks precipitants, hypermetropia and drug triggers

model.text: I’m long-sighted, yes. Nothing new that I can think of, I’d have to look at my tablets.
Do you wear contact lenses, or have you had an injury to the eye?
No.
You wondered about a migraine or a bug. What worries you most right now?
The pain, and my sight. I’ve never had haloes before. I was hoping for something to stop it.

I don’t think this is a migraine or a bug. The painful red eye, the misty vision and the haloes together suggest the pressure inside the eye has suddenly gone very high. It’s called acute angle-closure glaucoma, and it can make you feel sick and give you a headache too.
model.why: Names the diagnosis and explains the misleading symptoms

model.text: Is it serious?

It is an emergency, because high pressure can damage the sight within hours. The good news is that eye specialists can bring the pressure down quickly, and treating it straight away gives the best chance of protecting your vision.
model.why: Honest about urgency, balanced with hope

model.text: Okay. What do I do?
You need to go to the emergency eye department now. I’ll phone them straight after this call so they’re expecting you, and send over what we’ve discussed.
Please don’t drive. Is there someone who can take you right away? If not, I’ll arrange an ambulance.
I’ll find out who can take me.

Let me know within the next few minutes, and I’ll call an ambulance if no one can. Take your glasses and a list or photo of your tablets. They’ll give you treatment for the pressure, the pain and the sickness when you arrive.
Please don’t use any eye drops or new medicines before you’re seen unless the eye team tells you to.
model.why: Avoids drugs that might worsen angle closure

model.text: If you can’t get there quickly, the vomiting won’t stop, or you feel faint or confused, call 999. Can you tell me what you’re going to do now?
Get a lift to the eye department now, don’t drive, take my tablets list, and call 999 if I can’t get there.
Exactly right. I’ll ring the eye department now and call you tomorrow to see how you are.

social.t: She is in pain, vomiting and has reduced vision in one eye. Confirm who can take her immediately, and call an ambulance if nobody can.
Laser treatment is usually offered to both eyes. She may need help with daily tasks for a short time and follow-up at the eye clinic.

legal.t: She must not drive today. Once treated, the eye team will advise; DVLA rules for glaucoma depend on whether the visual standards are met and whether both eyes are affected (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: Be honest about what a video call can show. Document what was seen and what could not be assessed, and escalate on history (GMC Good medical practice).
After the episode, review medicines with antimuscarinic or sympathomimetic effects, and code the diagnosis so future prescribers are alerted.

community.t: Close relatives may be at higher risk of angle closure; the eye team can advise whether they should have an eye examination.

redFlags: Painful red eye with reduced vision
Headache and vomiting with eye pain
Mid-dilated, unreactive pupil or hazy cornea (if seen)
Recent new antimuscarinic, sympathomimetic, antidepressant or topiramate treatment, or dilating drops
ice: Idea: a migraine or a sickness bug
Concern: the pain and her vision
Expectation: something to stop the pain and sickness

playbook.diagnosis: “The painful red eye, the misty vision and the haloes point to the pressure inside your eye going suddenly very high. It’s called acute angle-closure glaucoma, and it needs treatment today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Fluid inside the eye normally drains out through a small channel. In your eye that channel has suddenly closed, like a plug over a drain, so the pressure builds up. The eye team can open the drain again.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered about a migraine or a bug, which is understandable with the headache and sickness. But the eye is the key, and it needs the eye department now.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange immediate transport, with an ambulance if nobody can take her, and follow up the next day.
sharedPlan: Emergency eye department now, with phone handover
No driving; ambulance if no lift within minutes
Take glasses and a medicine list
No new drops or medicines until seen
Medicines review and follow-up call after treatment
safetyNet: 999 if she cannot get there quickly, the vomiting continues, or she feels faint or confused
GP follow-up call the next day

pitfalls.intro: This station hides an eye emergency behind a headache and vomiting. The marks go to the candidate who recognises the pattern quickly, admits what video cannot show, and gets her to the eye department now.

items.why: Misses a sight-threatening emergency. Migraine does not cause a red eye with reduced vision and haloes.
items.fix: Ask about the eye first: redness, vision, haloes.

items.fail: Referring to an optician or a routine clinic.
items.why: Acute angle closure is a same-day emergency (College of Optometrists); sight can be lost within hours.
items.fix: Emergency eye department now, with a phone handover.

items.fail: Claiming to examine the pupil or pressure on video.
items.why: Over-claiming an examination is unsafe and undermines credibility.
items.fix: Say what you can see and what you cannot, and act on the history.

items.why: Antimuscarinic, sympathomimetic and some antidepressant drugs, dilating drops and topiramate can precipitate angle closure.
items.fix: Ask about new tablets and drops, and review them after treatment.

items.why: A frightened patient in pain needs clarity and reassurance that treatment works.
items.fix: “It’s an emergency, and the eye team can bring the pressure down quickly.”

items.fail: Letting her drive or leaving transport vague.
items.why: She has reduced vision, pain and vomiting.
items.fix: No driving; a lift now or an ambulance.

items.why: Delays at the front door cost sight.
items.fix: Phone the eye department, then follow up the next day.

timeMap.d: Acknowledge the pain and agree a short, focused consultation.
Unilateral, reduced vision, deep ache vs gritty, photophobia, dim-light onset, long sight, new drugs or drops, contact lenses. Look at the eye on camera and say what you cannot assess.
Migraine or bug, fear for her sight, wanting relief.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma; why it causes vomiting; emergency but treatable.
Emergency eye department now with a phone handover, no driving, ambulance if no lift, 999 triggers, teach-back and next-day follow-up.

wordPics.fail: Labels it migraine or gastroenteritis and advises an antiemetic and painkillers; or suspects glaucoma but books an optician or a routine referral; claims to examine the pressure or pupil on video.
wordPics.pass: Recognises acute angle-closure glaucoma from the history, explains it is an emergency, and arranges immediate transfer to the emergency eye department without driving.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains why the headache and vomiting misled her; is honest about the limits of the video look; checks drug precipitants; hands over directly and sets a time limit for arranging transport; balances urgency with hope; uses teach-back and follows up.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like a migraine. Take something for the sickness and rest in a dark room.”
avoid.instead: “A migraine doesn’t make the eye red and misty. This looks like high pressure in the eye, and you need the eye department now.”
avoid.why: A dark room dilates the pupil and can worsen angle closure; delay risks the sight.

avoid.dont: “I can see your pupil isn’t reacting and the eye is hard.”
avoid.instead: “I can see the eye is very red. I can’t check the pressure on video, but your symptoms fit.”
avoid.why: Pressure and pupil reactions cannot be examined on video; over-claiming is unsafe and unprofessional.

avoid.dont: “Get your optician to have a look in the next few days.”
avoid.instead: “You need to be seen in the emergency eye department now. I’ll call them.”
avoid.why: Acute angle closure needs same-day treatment within hours.

professional.t: Be honest about what a video call can show. Document what was seen and what could not be assessed, and escalate on history (GMC Good medical practice).
After the episode, review medicines with antimuscarinic or sympathomimetic effects, and code the diagnosis so future prescribers are alerted.

community.t: Close relatives may be at higher risk of angle closure; the eye team can advise whether they should have an eye examination.

redFlags: Painful red eye with reduced vision
Headache and vomiting with eye pain
Mid-dilated, unreactive pupil or hazy cornea (if seen)
Recent new antimuscarinic, sympathomimetic, antidepressant or topiramate treatment, or dilating drops
ice: Idea: a migraine or a sickness bug
Concern: the pain and her vision
Expectation: something to stop the pain and sickness

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The painful red eye, the misty vision and the haloes point to the pressure inside your eye going suddenly very high. It’s called acute angle-closure glaucoma, and it needs treatment today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Fluid inside the eye normally drains out through a small channel. In your eye that channel has suddenly closed, like a plug over a drain, so the pressure builds up. The eye team can open the drain again.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered about a migraine or a bug, which is understandable with the headache and sickness. But the eye is the key, and it needs the eye department now.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange immediate transport, with an ambulance if nobody can take her, and follow up the next day.
sharedPlan: Emergency eye department now, with phone handover
No driving; ambulance if no lift within minutes
Take glasses and a medicine list
No new drops or medicines until seen
Medicines review and follow-up call after treatment
safetyNet: 999 if she cannot get there quickly, the vomiting continues, or she feels faint or confused
GP follow-up call the next day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station hides an eye emergency behind a headache and vomiting. The marks go to the candidate who recognises the pattern quickly, admits what video cannot show, and gets her to the eye department now.

items.why: Misses a sight-threatening emergency. Migraine does not cause a red eye with reduced vision and haloes.
items.fix: Ask about the eye first: redness, vision, haloes.

items.fail: Referring to an optician or a routine clinic.
items.why: Acute angle closure is a same-day emergency (College of Optometrists); sight can be lost within hours.
items.fix: Emergency eye department now, with a phone handover.

items.fail: Claiming to examine the pupil or pressure on video.
items.why: Over-claiming an examination is unsafe and undermines credibility.
items.fix: Say what you can see and what you cannot, and act on the history.

items.why: Antimuscarinic, sympathomimetic and some antidepressant drugs, dilating drops and topiramate can precipitate angle closure.
items.fix: Ask about new tablets and drops, and review them after treatment.

items.why: A frightened patient in pain needs clarity and reassurance that treatment works.
items.fix: “It’s an emergency, and the eye team can bring the pressure down quickly.”

items.fail: Letting her drive or leaving transport vague.
items.why: She has reduced vision, pain and vomiting.
items.fix: No driving; a lift now or an ambulance.

items.why: Delays at the front door cost sight.
items.fix: Phone the eye department, then follow up the next day.
